claims.evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: nhr-14 encodes a protein homologous to the HNF4 family of nuclear receptors.
claims.source: nhr-14 is predicted to encode a protein homologous to the HNF4 family of nuclear receptors, which are transcription factors that regulate gene expression in response to nutritional, metabolic and environmental signals (Taubert et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Taubert et al., 2011 and sequence analysis.

claims.claim: NHR-14 has a highly conserved N-terminal zinc finger DNA-binding domain.
claims.source: Amino acid sequence alignment between NHR-14 and human HNF4α showed a highly conserved N-terminal zinc finger DNA-binding domain (DBD) and a conserved C-terminal ligand-binding domain (LBD) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: NHR-14 has a conserved C-terminal ligand-binding domain.
claims.source: Amino acid sequence alignment between NHR-14 and human HNF4α showed a highly conserved N-terminal zinc finger DNA-binding domain (DBD) and a conserved C-terminal ligand-binding domain (LBD) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The qa6909 mutation is predicted to result in a truncated protein that lacks a significant portion of the DBD and the entire LBD.
claims.source: The qa6909 mutation (Trp49STOP) located within the DBD is predicted to result in a truncated protein that lacks a significant portion of the DBD and the entire LBD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the location of the stop codon mutation in the protein sequence.

claims.claim: Gly33 is conserved in HNF4 receptors found in vertebrates and Drosophila.
claims.source: Gly33 is conserved in HNF4 receptors found in vertebrates and Drosophila, and it is likely that this substitution disrupts DNA binding.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claims.claim: The Gly33Arg substitution likely disrupts DNA binding.
claims.source: Gly33 is conserved in HNF4 receptors found in vertebrates and Drosophila, and it is likely that this substitution disrupts DNA binding.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the nature of the amino acid substitution and its location in the DNA-binding domain.

claims.claim: The tm1473 mutation is a 409 bp deletion of the third exon and intron that results in a premature stop codon and deletion of the ligand-binding domain.
claims.source: The tm1473 mutation is a 409 bp deletion of the third exon and intron that results in a premature stop codon and deletion of the ligand-binding domain that likely results in nhr-14 loss of function.
claims.evidence: This is based on molecular characterization of the tm1473 allele.

claims.claim: hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants developed normally under iron limitation.
claims.source: hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants developed normally under iron limitation (Figure 1D), showing that loss of nhr-14 function is responsible for the rescue observed in qa6909 and qa6910 mutant animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: NHR-14::GFP::FLAG is highly expressed in intestinal nuclei and in cells in the head.
claims.source: Fluorescent imaging of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG worms showed that it is highly expressed in intestinal nuclei and in cells in the head (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: No significant change in levels of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG was observed in wild-type N2 worms grown in low iron or high iron compared to NGM.
claims.source: No significant change in levels of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG and nhr-14 mRNA were observed in wild-type N2 worms grown in low iron (NGM-BP) or high iron (NGM- ferric ammonium citrate, FAC) compared to NGM (Figure 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claims.claim: No significant change in nhr-14 mRNA was observed in wild-type N2 worms grown in low iron or high iron compared to NGM.
claims.source: No significant change in levels of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG and nhr-14 mRNA were observed in wild-type N2 worms grown in low iron (NGM-BP) or high iron (NGM- ferric ammonium citrate, FAC) compared to NGM (Figure 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Nuclear localization of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG was not affected by iron or by BP.
claims.source: Furthermore, nuclear localization of NHR-14::GFP::FLAG was not affected by iron or by BP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 834 differentially expressed genes changed at least two-fold in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms at a 5% FDR.
claims.source: We identified 834 differentially expressed genes that changed at least two-fold compared to wild-type N2 worms at a 5% false discovery rate (FDR), 573 of which were upregulated and 261 downregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claims.claim: 573 genes were upregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We identified 834 differentially expressed genes that changed at least two-fold compared to wild-type N2 worms at a 5% false discovery rate (FDR), 573 of which were upregulated and 261 downregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claims.claim: 261 genes were downregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We identified 834 differentially expressed genes that changed at least two-fold compared to wild-type N2 worms at a 5% false discovery rate (FDR), 573 of which were upregulated and 261 downregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claims.claim: smf-3 is one of the most highly upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.source: Notably, the primary intestinal iron transporter smf-3 is one of the most highly upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: smf-3 is upregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We confirmed smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants and in hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms, and smf-3 downregulation in hif-1(ia4) mutants by qPCR (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: smf-3 is upregulated in hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We confirmed smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants and in hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms, and smf-3 downregulation in hif-1(ia4) mutants by qPCR (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: smf-3 is downregulated in hif-1(ia4) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We confirmed smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants and in hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms, and smf-3 downregulation in hif-1(ia4) mutants by qPCR (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: hif-1(ia4) and smf-3(ok1035) mutants displayed reduced iron content compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous study, hif-1(ia4) and smf-3(ok1035) mutants displayed reduced iron content compared to wild-type N2 worms (Romney et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ICP-OES data shown in Figure 3B and cited previous work.

claims.claim: Iron content increased in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.source: Iron content increased in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants consistent with increased smf-3 expression, and decreased in smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ICP-OES data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Iron content decreased in smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants.
claims.source: Iron content increased in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants consistent with increased smf-3 expression, and decreased in smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ICP-OES data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: smf-3(ok1035) single mutants display a developmental delay under iron limitation.
claims.source: smf-3(ok1035) single mutants, smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants and smf-3(ok1035); hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) triple mutants also displayed a developmental delay under iron limitation showing that smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants is required for the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants display a developmental delay under iron limitation.
claims.source: smf-3(ok1035) single mutants, smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants and smf-3(ok1035); hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) triple mutants also displayed a developmental delay under iron limitation showing that smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants is required for the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: smf-3(ok1035); hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) triple mutants display a developmental delay under iron limitation.
claims.source: smf-3(ok1035) single mutants, smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants and smf-3(ok1035); hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) triple mutants also displayed a developmental delay under iron limitation showing that smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants is required for the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants is required for the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants.
claims.source: smf-3(ok1035) single mutants, smf-3(ok1035); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants and smf-3(ok1035); hif-1(ia4); nhr-14(tm1473) triple mutants also displayed a developmental delay under iron limitation showing that smf-3 upregulation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants is required for the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: nhr-14(tm1473) mutants have a survival advantage when grown in low iron compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: Further evidence for SMF-3-mediated iron uptake as a mechanism to explain the rescue of hif-1(ia4) mutants under iron limitation is the survival advantage of nhr-14(tm1473) mutants grown in low iron (BP) as compared to wild-type N2 worms (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: NHR-14 is a negative regulator of SMF-3-mediated iron uptake.
claims.source: Collectively, these results are consistent with NHR-14 as a negative regulator of SMF-3-mediated iron uptake.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined genetic, expression, and iron content data.

claims.claim: GFP expression increased with BP in control-RNAi fed Psmf-3::GFP-H2B worms.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous study (Romney et al., 2011), GFP expression increased with BP and decreased with FAC in control-RNAi fed worms, reflecting HIF-1 regulation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by COPAS Biosort data shown in Figure 4B and cited previous work.

claims.claim: GFP expression decreased with FAC in control-RNAi fed Psmf-3::GFP-H2B worms.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous study (Romney et al., 2011), GFP expression increased with BP and decreased with FAC in control-RNAi fed worms, reflecting HIF-1 regulation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by COPAS Biosort data shown in Figure 4B and cited previous work.

claims.claim: GFP expression is increased in nhr-14-RNAi fed Psmf-3::GFP-H2B worms with NGM, NGM-BP and NGM-FAC treatments.
claims.source: GFP expression is further increased in nhr-14-RNAi fed worms with NGM, NGM-BP and NGM-FAC treatments, indicating that sequences within the smf-3 promoter are important for NHR-14 regulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by COPAS Biosort data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Sequences within the smf-3 promoter are important for NHR-14 regulation.
claims.source: GFP expression is further increased in nhr-14-RNAi fed worms with NGM, NGM-BP and NGM-FAC treatments, indicating that sequences within the smf-3 promoter are important for NHR-14 regulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay data.

claims.claim: PQM-1 showed significant association with the smf-3 IDE.
claims.source: We found that the transcription factor PQM-1 showed significant association with the smf-3 IDE (IV: 2618542..2619063; qValue 1.7e−32), suggesting that PQM-1 might be involved in smf-3 activation in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of published ChIP-seq data from Wormbase.

claims.claim: PQM-1 associates with a GATA-like motif (TGATAAG) termed the DAF-16-associated element (DAE).
claims.source: PQM-1 associates with a GATA-like motif (TGATAAG) termed the DAF-16-associated element (DAE) found in the promoters of DAF-16/FoxO-Class II genes (Tepper et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tepper et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Single mutations in DAE 1, 2 or 3 motifs were associated with reduced GFP expression in untreated and BP-treated worms compared to Psmf-3::GFP-H2B worms carrying wildtype DAEs.
claims.source: Single mutations in DAE 1, 2 or 3 motifs (TGATAAG to TCATAAG) were associated with reduced GFP expression in untreated and BP-treated worms compared to Psmf-3::GFP-H2B worms carrying wildtype DAEs (Figure 4C—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by COPAS Biosort data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Endogenous smf-3 expression was reduced in pqm-1(ok485) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: Endogenous smf-3 expression was also reduced in pqm-1(ok485) mutants compared to wild-type N2 worms (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: smf-3 expression was reduced in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants fed pqm-1 RNAi.
claims.source: Further evidence suggesting that PQM-1 activates smf-3 was shown by reduced smf-3 expression in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants fed pqm-1 RNAi (Figure 4E) and by the low iron developmental delay observed in pqm-1(ok485) mutants (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: pqm-1(ok485) mutants display a low iron developmental delay.
claims.source: Further evidence suggesting that PQM-1 activates smf-3 was shown by reduced smf-3 expression in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants fed pqm-1 RNAi (Figure 4E) and by the low iron developmental delay observed in pqm-1(ok485) mutants (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: PQM-1::GFP::FLAG localized to nuclei in intestinal cells in L4 stage worms fed either control RNAi or nhr-14 RNAi.
claims.source: In agreement with these studies, PQM-1::GFP::FLAG localized to nuclei in intestinal cells in L4 stage worms fed either control RNAi or nhr-14 RNAi, and to the cytoplasm in adults fed control RNAi.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: PQM-1::GFP::FLAG localized to the cytoplasm in adults fed control RNAi.
claims.source: In agreement with these studies, PQM-1::GFP::FLAG localized to nuclei in intestinal cells in L4 stage worms fed either control RNAi or nhr-14 RNAi, and to the cytoplasm in adults fed control RNAi.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: PQM-1::GFP::FLAG remained in intestinal nuclei in adult worms fed nhr-14-RNAi.
claims.source: PQM-1::GFP::FLAG, however, remained in intestinal nuclei in adult worms fed nhr-14-RNAi (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: PQM-1 activates smf-3 by associating with GATA-like DAE motifs in the smf-3 promoter.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that PQM-1 activates smf-3 by associating with GATA-like DAE motifs in the smf-3 promoter, and that NHR-14 acts upstream of PQM-1 to inhibit its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP-seq, reporter, and genetic data.

claims.claim: NHR-14 acts upstream of PQM-1 to inhibit its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that PQM-1 activates smf-3 by associating with GATA-like DAE motifs in the smf-3 promoter, and that NHR-14 acts upstream of PQM-1 to inhibit its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and localization data showing PQM-1 nuclear retention in nhr-14 mutants.

claims.claim: Upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants were involved in the innate immune response.
claims.source: Gene-set enrichment analysis using gene ontology (GO) terms (Huang et al., 2009) showed that upregulated genes were involved in the innate immune response (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Over-represented functional categories in upregulated nhr-14 genes included C-type lectin, CUB-domain proteins, lysosomes, peptidases, glutathione S-transferases and collagens.
claims.source: Over-represented functional categories within this dataset included C-type lectin (carbohydrate binding proteins), CUB-domain proteins (extracellular and membrane proteins), lysosomes, peptidases, glutathione S-transferases (xenobiotic metabolism) and collagens, all of which are part of a core immune response program in C. elegans (Simonsen et al., 2012) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DAVID analysis shown in Figure 5C and cited reference.

claims.claim: A GATA motif was found in 341 out of 573 upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.source: An unbiased search for cis-regulatory elements in the 1 kb promotor regions of upregulated and downregulated nhr-14 genes revealed the presence of a GATA motif in 341 out of 573 upregulated genes and a tandem-direct repeat motif in 14 out of 261 downregulated genes (Figure 5F and Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: A tandem-direct repeat motif was found in 14 out of 261 downregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.source: An unbiased search for cis-regulatory elements in the 1 kb promotor regions of upregulated and downregulated nhr-14 genes revealed the presence of a GATA motif in 341 out of 573 upregulated genes and a tandem-direct repeat motif in 14 out of 261 downregulated genes (Figure 5F and Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: There is overlap between genes upregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants and genes upregulated in response to P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: We found overlap between genes upregulated in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants and genes upregulated in response to P. aeruginosa (Shapira et al., 2006; Troemel et al., 2006), S. aureus (Visvikis et al., 2014), Pseudomonas luminescens (Wong et al., 2007), Enterococcus faecalis (Wong et al., 2007) and Serratia marcescens (Engelmann et al., 2011) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—source data 1).

claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis with published datasets shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: There is expression overlap between nhr-14 RNA-seq dataset and DAF-2/DAF-16 pathway genes.
claims.source: We compared our nhr-14 RNA-seq dataset with p38-MAPK (Troemel et al., 2006), TGFβ (Roberts et al., 2010), ELT-2 (Block et al., 2015) and DAF-2/DAF-16 (Murphy et al., 2003) innate immune pathway datasets, and found expression overlap with these pathways (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source datas 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis with published datasets shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: PQM-1 showed significant association to 15 out of the top 25 upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants.
claims.source: Analysis of ChIP-seq data revealed significant PQM-1 association to 15 out of the top 25 upregulated genes in nhr-14(tm1473) mutants, while only 3 out of 25 for the downregulated subset showed significant PQM-1 association (Niu et al., 2011) (Figure 6—source data 3).

claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of published ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Expression of dod-19, dod-24, clec-41, gst-38 and oac-14 was reduced in nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants compared with nhr-14(tm1473); control RNAi worms.
claims.source: qPCR analysis showed reduced expression of Class II genes dod-19, dod-24, clec-41, gst-38 and oac-14 in nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants compared with nhr-14(tm1473); control RNAi worms.

claims.claim: The Class II genes ins-7 and lys-2 were not changed in nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants.

claims.claim: The Class I genes lys-7 and ftn-1 were not changed in nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants.

claims.claim: nhr-14(tm1473) mutants displayed enhanced resistance to PA14 infection compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type N2 worms, nhr-14(tm1473) mutants displayed enhanced resistance to PA14 infection, while smf-3(ok1035) mutants were hypersensitive (Figure 8A and Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: smf-3(ok1035) mutants were hypersensitive to PA14 infection compared to wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type N2 worms, nhr-14(tm1473) mutants displayed enhanced resistance to PA14 infection, while smf-3(ok1035) mutants were hypersensitive (Figure 8A and Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: smf-3(ok485); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants displayed increased resistance to PA14 compared to smf-3(ok1035) single mutants.
claims.source: smf-3(ok485); nhr-14(tm1473) double mutants displayed increased resistance to PA14 compared to smf-3(ok1035) single mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: nhr-14 partially suppresses the sensitivity of smf-3(ok1035) to PA14.

claims.claim: Other genes in addition to smf-3 contribute to the resistance of nhr-14(tm1473) mutants to PA14.

claims.claim: pqm-1(ok485) mutants displayed similar sensitivity to P. aeruginosa PA14 as wild-type N2 worms.
claims.source: We also analyzed the resistance of the pqm-1(ok485) single mutant and nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants to PA14. pqm-1(ok485) mutants displayed a wild-type sensitivity to PA14.
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants were more sensitive to PA14 than nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants.

claims.evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: PQM-1 is required for nhr-14(tm1473) enhanced PA14 resistance.
claims.source: nhr-14(tm1473); pqm-1 RNAi mutants were more sensitive to PA14 than nhr-14(tm1473) single mutants, indicating that PQM-1 is required for nhr-14(tm1473) enhanced PA14 resistance (Figure 8A and Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis data.

claims.claim: PA14 exposure repressed nhr-14 in wild-type N2 worms.

claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: PA14 exposure repressed ftn-1 in wild-type N2 worms.

claims.claim: PA14 exposure induced smf-3 in wild-type N2 worms.

results.result: Loss of function mutations in nhr-14, a nuclear receptor encoding gene homologous to HNF4, rescue the developmental delay of hif-1 mutants under iron limitation. Two independent alleles (qa6909 and qa6910) were identified through a suppressor screen, with qa6909 introducing a premature stop codon (Trp49STOP) and qa6910 causing a missense mutation (Gly33Arg) in the conserved DNA-binding domain. A third allele (tm1473) with a 409 bp deletion also rescues the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C33-C42 provide converging genetic evidence from multiple independent alleles (qa6909, qa6910, tm1473) that loss of nhr-14 function rescues hif-1 mutant developmental delay under iron limitation. The molecular characterization of mutations (C33-C41) and rescue validation with tm1473 (C42) strongly support this result. The genetic screen methodology and phenotypic rescue are well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: NHR-14 is highly expressed in intestinal nuclei and head cells, and its expression and localization are not regulated by iron availability. Western blot and qPCR analyses show no significant changes in NHR-14::GFP::FLAG protein or nhr-14 mRNA levels when worms are grown under low iron (BP) or high iron (FAC) conditions compared to normal growth medium.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by confocal microscopy (C43), Western blot (C44), qPCR (C45), and additional microscopy data (C46) showing consistent NHR-14 expression and localization across iron conditions. The use of a functional fosmid-based reporter (validated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and multiple complementary techniques strengthen this conclusion. Statistical analyses indicate no significant differences.

results.result: Loss of nhr-14 upregulates the intestinal metal transporter SMF-3, leading to increased iron uptake. RNA-seq identified smf-3 as one of the most highly upregulated genes in nhr-14 mutants, confirmed by qPCR. Iron content measurements show increased iron in nhr-14 mutants and decreased iron in smf-3; nhr-14 double mutants. Genetic epistasis experiments demonstrate that smf-3 upregulation is required for rescue of hif-1 mutants under iron limitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C50-C56, C60, C62 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: RNA-seq (C50), qPCR validation (C51-C53), ICP-OES iron measurements (C54-C56), and genetic epistasis showing smf-3 dependence (C57-C60). The convergence of transcriptional, biochemical, and genetic data provides robust support for NHR-14 as a negative regulator of SMF-3-mediated iron uptake.

results.result: smf-3 is required for the rescue of hif-1 mutants by nhr-14 loss under iron limitation, and nhr-14 mutants show enhanced survival under low iron conditions. Developmental delay assays show that smf-3(ok1035) single, double, and triple mutants all display developmental delays under iron limitation, and nhr-14(tm1473) mutants have a survival advantage in low iron compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59, C61 are supported by developmental assays (Figure 3C) and survival analysis (Figure 3D). The genetic epistasis experiments with multiple mutant combinations provide clear evidence that smf-3 is required for the nhr-14 rescue phenotype. The survival advantage of nhr-14 mutants under low iron further supports the functional importance of this pathway.

results.result: PQM-1 activates smf-3 transcription by binding to GATA-like DAE (DAF-16-associated element) motifs in the smf-3 promoter. ChIP-seq analysis shows PQM-1 association with the smf-3 iron-dependent element (IDE). Reporter assays with mutated DAE motifs show reduced GFP expression, and pqm-1 mutants show reduced endogenous smf-3 expression and developmental delay under low iron. RNAi knockdown of pqm-1 in nhr-14 mutants reduces smf-3 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72, C76 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: ChIP-seq data analysis (C67), reporter assays with DAE mutations (C69), qPCR of endogenous smf-3 in pqm-1 mutants (C70-C71), and developmental assays (C72). The convergence of ChIP-seq, reporter, genetic, and expression data provides strong evidence for PQM-1 as a direct transcriptional activator of smf-3 through DAE motifs.

results.result: NHR-14 regulates PQM-1 subcellular localization. PQM-1::GFP::FLAG localizes to intestinal nuclei in L4 larvae but becomes cytoplasmic in adults under normal conditions. However, in nhr-14 RNAi-treated adults, PQM-1 remains nuclear, suggesting NHR-14 acts upstream of PQM-1 to inhibit its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C77 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 4G) showing developmental stage-specific and nhr-14-dependent PQM-1 localization. The retention of PQM-1 in adult nuclei upon nhr-14 knockdown provides clear evidence for NHR-14's role in regulating PQM-1 localization. This is consistent with prior literature on PQM-1 localization patterns and provides a mechanistic link between NHR-14 and PQM-1.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of nhr-14(tm1473) mutants reveals 834 differentially expressed genes (573 upregulated, 261 downregulated) at 5% FDR with at least 2-fold change. Gene ontology analysis shows enrichment for innate immune response genes, including C-type lectins, CUB-domain proteins, lysosomes, peptidases, glutathione S-transferases, and collagens. Motif analysis reveals GATA motifs in 341/573 upregulated genes and tandem-direct repeat motifs in 14/261 downregulated genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49, C78-C81 are supported by RNA-seq data with appropriate statistical thresholds (5% FDR, 2-fold change). GO enrichment analysis (C78-C79) and unbiased motif discovery (C80-C81) provide functional context. The enrichment of GATA motifs in upregulated genes is consistent with PQM-1-mediated regulation. The RNA-seq methodology appears sound with biological replicates.

results.result: nhr-14 mutants display increased expression of innate immune genes and DAF-16/FoxO-Class II genes. Comparative analysis shows overlap with genes induced by various pathogens and with p38-MAPK, TGFβ, ELT-2, and DAF-2/DAF-16 immune pathways. ChIP-seq analysis reveals PQM-1 association with 15/25 top upregulated genes. qPCR validation shows that some Class II genes (dod-19, dod-24, clec-41, gst-38, oac-14) require PQM-1 for expression in nhr-14 mutants, while others (ins-7, lys-2, lys-7, ftn-1) do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C82-C91 are supported by RNA-seq data, comparative analysis with published datasets, ChIP-seq analysis, and qPCR validation. The overlap with pathogen-induced genes and known immune pathways provides biological context. The differential PQM-1 dependence of Class II genes (C89-C91) suggests complexity in regulation and is appropriately acknowledged. The use of multiple validation approaches strengthens these findings.

results.result: nhr-14 mutants display enhanced resistance to P. aeruginosa PA14 infection, while smf-3 mutants are hypersensitive. The resistance of nhr-14 mutants is partially dependent on smf-3 and requires PQM-1. smf-3; nhr-14 double mutants show intermediate resistance compared to smf-3 single mutants, suggesting additional genes contribute to nhr-14-mediated pathogen resistance. pqm-1 mutants show wild-type sensitivity to PA14, but pqm-1 RNAi in nhr-14 mutants reduces their enhanced resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C92-C99 are supported by survival analysis data (Figure 8A) with appropriate statistical testing (Log-rank Mantel-Cox test). The genetic epistasis experiments with multiple mutant combinations provide evidence for both smf-3-dependent and smf-3-independent mechanisms of pathogen resistance. The requirement for PQM-1 in nhr-14-mediated resistance is clearly demonstrated. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=47-78 per condition).

results.result: PA14 exposure represses nhr-14 and ftn-1 while inducing smf-3 and dod-24 in wild-type worms. NHR-14 protein levels decrease and PQM-1 accumulates in nuclei upon PA14 exposure. In nhr-14 mutants, PA14 induces smf-3, dod-24, and ftn-1 expression relative to wild-type levels, while these genes are repressed by PA14 in pqm-1 mutants. NHR-14 repression and PQM-1 are required for PA14 induction of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C112 are supported by qPCR (Figure 8B, 8E), Western blot (Figure 8C), and microscopy data (Figure 8D) showing coordinated responses to pathogen exposure. The genetic experiments in nhr-14 and pqm-1 mutants (C108-C111) demonstrate the requirement for both factors in pathogen-induced gene expression. The convergence of expression, protein, and localization data provides strong support for the proposed regulatory mechanism.

results.result: Iron content increases in wild-type worms exposed to PA14 and is further elevated in nhr-14 mutants. The low iron content in smf-3 mutants is unaffected by PA14 exposure. Iron content in pqm-1 mutants is lower than nhr-14 mutants and unaffected by PA14. NHR-14 repression and PQM-1 activation are required for PA14 induction of SMF-3-dependent iron uptake and FTN-1 iron storage, demonstrating iron sequestration as a component of innate immunity in C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C120 are supported by ICP-MS iron measurements (Figure 8F) across multiple genotypes and conditions. The genetic epistasis experiments clearly demonstrate the requirement for both NHR-14 repression and PQM-1 activation in pathogen-induced iron uptake. The integration of iron content data with gene expression and pathogen resistance data provides strong support for iron sequestration as an innate immune mechanism. Statistical analyses with appropriate replicates (n=3-5) strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: The authors propose a model whereby C. elegans respond to pathogen infection by reducing NHR-14 abundance, allowing PQM-1 nuclear translocation to activate genes critical for innate immunity and iron uptake. Loss of nhr-14 increases SMF-3-mediated iron uptake and induces innate immune response genes that contribute to pathogen resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 represent the integrated model supported by the collective data from genetic screens, expression analyses, localization studies, iron measurements, and pathogen resistance assays. The model is well-supported by the convergence of multiple experimental approaches. However, the mechanism by which pathogens trigger NHR-14 reduction remains to be determined, which the authors appropriately acknowledge in the Discussion.

results.result: Background claims establishing the importance of iron metabolism, the role of HIF-1 in C. elegans iron regulation, the conservation of iron metabolism proteins between C. elegans and mammals, and the role of iron in pathogen infections and innate immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C11-C32 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context for the study but do not represent novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Background claims about nuclear receptors, PQM-1 function, and DAF-16/FoxO signaling pathways in C. elegans, including the unique role of NHR-14 in coupling innate immunity with iron sequestration and the regulation of PQM-1 localization by various signaling pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C125-C138 are primarily background knowledge supported by appropriate citations, with some speculative elements (C127, C133, C138) that are appropriately qualified. The claims about PQM-1's known functions (C128-C132, C134-C136) are well-supported by citations. The speculation about NHR-14's unique role (C127) and additional regulatory pathways (C138) are reasonable inferences from the data but require further investigation.

results.result: Discussion claims comparing C. elegans iron sequestration mechanisms to vertebrate systems, discussing potential mechanisms of pathogen sensing, and evolutionary considerations regarding nuclear receptor conservation in nematodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C163 are primarily speculative discussion points (C139-C140, C149-C150, C159, C163) or background knowledge from literature (C141-C148, C151-C162). The speculative claims about mechanisms (C139-C140, C149-C150) are appropriately qualified but lack direct experimental support. The evolutionary comparisons (C159-C163) are interesting but speculative. The background claims about vertebrate systems (C141-C145) are well-cited but not directly tested in this study.
